item.title: How the construction, desecration and destruction of Jerusalem’s ancient temples shaped Judaism – and Hanukkah
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

In 167 B.C.E., on the 25th day of the Hebrew month of Kislev, the Greek king Antiochos IV Epiphanes entered the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem. According to tradition, he converted the sanctuary to a temple to Zeus. More broadly, Antiochos outlawed Jewish customs, including dietary laws, circumcision and observing the Sabbath.

The name Epiphanes meant “manifest,” implying the king was a god on Earth, but Jewish sources called him “Epimanes”: madman.

Three years later, on the same day of the same month, Jews in Jerusalem scored a major victory against the Greeks, and the Temple was converted back to a Jewish place of worship. Rabbinic texts written much later described how one day’s worth of oil, all that was left to rededicate the Temple, lasted for eight – the seeming miracle at the heart of the Hanukkah story.

The holiday’s name means “dedication,” highlighting the temple’s importance for Jewish cultures. This temple, in fact, was the second version, after the first place of worship to the Jewish deity was destroyed in 586 B.C.E..

As a scholar of the Bible and religions drawn from it, I am fascinated by the history of the two temples in Jerusalem, which are vital for understanding the background of Hanukkah.

The First Temple

In ancient West Asia, temples played a pivotal role in religion, politics, the economy and even family life. In many ways, for example, they functioned like modern banks, where taxes would be collected and storehouses of treasuries accumulated.

Temples also served as the house of the god or goddess worshipped there. At a temple at Ain Dara, in modern-day Syria, carvings of 10-foot-long (3-meter-long) footsteps represent a deity entering its abode. Several times, the Bible refers to the temple in Jerusalem as the “house of the LORD.”

The first major temple in Jerusalem is traditionally thought to have been built by King Solomon in the 10th century B.C.E. Nothing of Solomon’s temple remains, but the Bible’s Book of 1 Kings describes three main sections: an outer portico, a main hall and the “holy of holies,” an inner sanctuary.

The ancient Israelites’ belief that God resided in that sanctuary was foundational to the often-bewildering sets of rituals performed at the Temple. These laws, laid out in the biblical Book of Leviticus, were designed to keep the divine abode ritually pure.

After all, if the most powerful being ever lived in the Temple, keeping it clean, and keeping God happy there, would be of paramount importance. When the divine presence settled in the Temple, biblical authors claimed, Jerusalem could not be destroyed.

After Solomon’s reign, ancient Israel split into two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south, where Jerusalem lay. Assyrians, whose large empire lay to the east, conquered the north in the eighth century B.C.E., and before long, their armies tried to invade Jerusalem, too. They failed, fueling biblical writers’ conviction that Jerusalem was inviolable so long as God lived there.

But over the years, the Bible describes religious observance in Judah growing lax. As the Book of Ezekiel tells it, God departed his dwelling, leaving it open to destruction by the Babylonians in 586 B.C.E.

The Second Temple

In the ancient world, many cultures believed that when a temple was destroyed, the god who dwelt there lost a battle. The victors tended to cart away images of the conquered cultures’ deities, an act called “god-napping.” Some of those divinities would be absorbed into the conquering culture’s traditions.

After Judah’s defeat, its people were exiled to Babylon, where Iraq and Syria are today. Yet the exiled Judeans’ traditions did not disappear. Instead, they found ways to innovate. In place of the Temple and the sacrifices made there, they built houses of worship called “synagogues” and developed new services and prayers.

About 50 years later, however, the Judeans received a second chance to create a divine dwelling in Jerusalem. Cyrus, king of Persia, decreed that they could return and build a second temple.

When this new structure was erected around 520 B.C.E., it proved initially disappointing. According to the Bible’s Book of Ezra, those who had seen the First Temple wept for sorrow since the second was a pale reflection of the first.

Not that this was the only temple: There is archaeological evidence of one in Egypt in the fifth century B.C.E.; and another, even earlier, in Tel Motza, just a few miles from Solomon’s Temple. Scholars debate how temples were perceived in ancient Judah, since the Bible’s Book of Deuteronomy suggests that only the one temple in Jerusalem should exist.

Despite the evidence for these other temples, surviving Jewish tradition has only emphasized these two – the First and Second – in Jerusalem.

Expansion – and destruction

It was the Second Temple that became the object of Antiochus’ persecution – a persecution that, according to some scholars, was the first religiously motivated one in history. Prior empires in the region cared little for local religious observances, as long as subjects paid taxes to the central authorities.

One motivation behind Antiochus’ actions may have been economic: His empire was losing ground, and fast, in an expensive struggle against the Romans, whose power in the Mediterranean was quickly growing. Jewish communities paid a tax to the Temple in Jerusalem, so robbing its treasures may have been an attempt to replenish the empire’s depleted finances.

Ultimately the Jewish community in Jerusalem won out against Antiochus’ persecution. Over a century later, under King Herod, the Second Temple was expanded to become quite a marvel. Even Roman sources described it as a splendid edifice. His reconstruction project would continue long after his life, into the early 60s C.E.

Only a few years later, in 70, the Romans destroyed the Second Temple. The Western Wall of the compound survives today as a testimony to Herod’s expansive construction project.

Judaism without a temple…

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-25 01:27 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Voyager’s cosmic map of Earth’s location: Cute, but wrong
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Here in late 2026, an incredible milestone has been reached: the Voyager 1 spacecraft — humanity’s most distant spacecraft from Earth — has finally passed a distance of one light-day from us. Along with its twin, Voyager 2, these two spacecraft have left the confines of the Solar System and now traverse interstellar space, freely floating through the interstellar medium. Eventually, their radioactive sources will decay away that they’ll become entirely inoperable, but there’s a chance that someday, in the far future, an alien species will encounter and recover one or both of these ancient artifacts: humanity’s first foray into the Universe beyond our own Solar System.

Aboard each of these two Voyagers is a special message intended for anyone who’d find them, whether in the near or distant future: the Voyager golden record. Containing songs, images, and sounds of Earth, it was designed to be an information-laden cosmic time capsule, capable of being easily deciphered by any intelligent alien species to come upon it. It was meant as an introduction to Earth and humanity, with the vision of serving as a cultural ambassador for our planet.

Emblazoned on the cover of the record are a series of diagrams, including one that we thought was incredibly important at the time: a map of Earth’s location in the galaxy, as determined through the mapping of 14 radio-loud pulsars. Although the method used to locate Earth was, for its time, a very clever one, we now understand that it’s inherently flawed. Anyone who receives it will most likely be unable to track down where our planet is from the included information, making it a cute, but wrongheaded, artifact from our cosmic infancy.

The whole point of the golden record was that it would serve as sort of a “time capsule” of humanity and Earth: an attempt to reach out to whomever might be out there in the Universe and share with them a little bit about what our world is like and what humanity — at its best — is all about. Carl Sagan, cocreator of the golden record, put it as follows:

“We [are] a species endowed with hope and perseverance, at least a little intelligence, substantial generosity and a palpable zest to make contact with the cosmos.”

Today, despite our stumbles and missteps in the 49 years that have ensued since the launch of the dual Voyager spacecrafts, all of these things remain true.

Grateful for curious minds

At the time, pulsars were a relatively new discovery. The very first one had only been discovered back in 1967, when then-graduate student Jocelyn Bell (later Jocelyn Bell Burnell), while surveying the sky for quasars, instead found a surprising signal on her chart-recorder papers that she described as a “bit of scruff.” After digging into that signal, she found that it was a radio emitter that pulsed with great regularity. Initially named LGM-1, for “Little Green Man 1,” it was soon determined not to be a signal of alien origin at all, but rather a rapidly rotating neutron star that emitted radio pulses. Today, that neutron star is known as our first pulsar, and has the less-poetic name PSR B1919+21.

Bell Burnell herself was the one who showed that this was unlikely to be a signal from intelligent extraterrestrials, when she continued her work and found a similar signal originating from a different part of the sky. Thomas Gold suggested the origin of pulsars should be rapidly rotating neutron stars the year after they were first discovered, in 1968. Originally discovered in the radio band, pulsars were swiftly detected over a wide variety of wavelengths across the electromagnetic spectrum. The first optical pulsar was discovered in January of 1969, and in May of 1969 the first X-ray pulsar was discovered in the heart of the Crab Nebula: a pulsar that was known to emit radio waves since the year prior.

By the time the Voyager spacecraft were launched in 1977, there were a cumulative 149 pulsars that had been discovered, and pulsar evolution had also been detected. In late 1968, the Crab pulsar’s period was found to slowly increase, meaning that the pulsar was spinning down over time. In 1969, the first “glitch” in a pulsar system was detected: an instantaneous change in the pulse period of a pulsar. Pulse period decay was identified in many more pulsars, and as of 1977, the period of the known pulsars ranged from a little over 1 second to as fast as 33 pulses per second.

We also had a rudimentary picture — just ten years after their initial discovery — for how these pulsars worked. The idea was that a neutron star was spinning, and that a neutron star itself isn’t just a ball of neutrons, but rather is a core of dense neutrons surrounded by a thin shell of atomic nuclei, including a mix of protons and neutrons combined, and much lighter electrons as well. As the neutron star spins, the much heavier protons and the much lighter electrons separate, and wind up with slightly different distributions across the neutron star’s outer layers and surface.

Whenever you have a set of electric charges in motion, they’re going to produce a magnetic field. The more charges you have, the greater a charge separation you have, the greater the charge density you have, and the faster the charges move, the stronger the generated magnetic field will be. Whereas the Earth has a magnetic field of about 1 Gauss, the strongest permanent magnets we can generate have a field strength of around 14,000 Gauss, and the strongest laboratory electromagnets have a magnitude of around 300,000-500,000 Gauss, the strength of a rotating neutron star’s magnetic field can routinely reach or exceed 100 trillion Gauss (10 Gauss): incredibly strong magnetic fields.…

Source: Big Think | Published: 2026-11-25 07:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: California raised minimum wages for fast-food workers – here’s how it played out 2 years later
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries.

As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results.

In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate.

As a researcher of health and labor markets, I joined with economists David Neumark, Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs.

We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at.

For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%.

This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain.

The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own.

Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase. Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own.

In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027.

Smaller chains see an impact

The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists.

In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero.

More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run.

Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage?

We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures.

We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones.

For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period.

But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose.

How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones.

A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses.

Taking the longer view

First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%.

That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains.

Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage.…

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-24 13:14 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://theconversation.com/california-raised-minimum-wages-for-fast-food-workers-heres-how-it-played-out-2-years-later-294552

item.title: Bloody, brutal and growing: More states are adopting the firing squad as an execution method
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The U.S. Army is scheduled to execute Nidal Hasan on Dec. 3, 2026, after Hasan killed 12 soldiers and one civilian at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth got President Donald Trump’s approval to use the firing squad to put Hasan to death.

However, the U.S. military hasn’t used the firing squad since 1945. And the execution method has been minimally used outside the military, accounting for only six of 1,664 executions in the U.S. in the past 50 years. Since 1976, the firing squad has been used in only two states: South Carolina and Utah.

The infrequency of its use might seem surprising to many Americans. After all, the firing squad is the least complicated execution method ever used in the U.S. All that is needed are guns, bullets and marksmen.

Still, it has not caught on throughout America’s history. And as a scholar of execution methods, I know why. Firing squad executions are bloody and brutal, and the U.S. has been more comfortable using methods that appear more humane.

History of firing squads in the US

The first use of a firing squad in what eventually became the U.S. occurred in 1608 in the English settlement of Jamestown. George Kendal, a British naval officer, was tried, convicted and sentenced to death for mutiny and treason. He was shot rather than hanged because of his high social standing. It was thought of as a more honorable way to die.

In 1996, a group of archaeologists found the skeleton of a young man in the walls of the original Jamestown fort, in what is modern-day Virginia. The skeleton showed signs of several gunshot wounds, and the archaeologists suspected it was Kendall’s remains.

The firing squad was used in the American Revolution to punish desertion. During the Civil War, both sides used it to create a “public spectacle, a vision of terror” to discourage desertion.

The U.S. Supreme Court in 1878 upheld the constitutionality of firing squad executions. Firing squads, the court decided, would not bring the sort of “terror, pain and disgrace” that would violate the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.

Nonetheless, after the Civil War and into the early 20th century, the firing squad was used only in Utah and Nevada. In 1913, Nevada built a device that fired three guns by pulling strings. The move came after the state had trouble finding volunteers to serve on firing squads.

20th-century firing squad executions

In 1915, labor activist Joe Hill was put to death in Utah by firing squad after being convicted of murdering three people. Hill had been a very vocal critic of capitalism and what he called the “greedy master class.” Some of his sympathizers claimed he was murdered as much for his activism as for his crimes.

As The Salt Lake Tribune noted in 2015, “Joe Hill was tied to a chair. Blindfolded. A small target was pinned to his chest. ‘Let it go, fire,’ he yelled. Rifles protruding from the blacksmith shop at Utah’s state prison obliged. Three of the bullets pierced his heart. The fourth went a little wide.”

In 1951, a firing squad execution in Utah went awry when the state put Eliseo J. Mares to death. He had been sentenced for the 1946 murder of an Ohio sailor who was killed while traveling to California for his marriage. Two of the four bullets missed Mares’s heart. They hit his hip and abdomen. He did not die quickly.

In January 1977, Utah also killed Gary Gilmore by firing squad. Utah law allowed prisoners to choose hanging or firing squad as execution methods. Gilmore elected the latter, saying it would allow him to “die with dignity.”

Gilmore was the first person executed in the U.S. after the Supreme Court‘s 1976 ruling that the death penalty was not a cruel and unusual punishment.

As Time magazine reported, “His neck, waist, wrists and feet were loosely bound to the chair. Twenty-six feet away hung a sailcloth partition with five slits. Hidden behind the curtain stood five riflemen armed with .30-.30 deer rifles, four loaded with steel-jacketed shells, the fifth with a blank.”

Gilmore’s last words: “Let’s do it.”

Is the firing squad humane?

I believe the firing squad has not played a large role in America’s death penalty history because it’s offensive to this country’s evolving standards of decency.

As an anesthesiologist told The Associated Press in March 2023, “Inmates could remain conscious for up to 10 seconds after being shot depending on where bullets strike … and those seconds could be ‘severely painful, especially related to shattering of bone and damage to the spinal cord.’”

States abandoned the firing squad because it was thought to mimic the violence to which executions were responding.

But Hasan’s execution comes at a time of revived interest in firing squads as an execution method, aided by continuing problems with lethal injection. They are now legal in five states: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.

Idaho is the only state that designates the firing squad as its primary execution method. Idaho state Rep. Bruce Skaug has called the method “certain” and “quick.”

Others agree. In a 2017 opinion, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote, “In addition to being near instant, death by shooting may also be comparatively painless.”

And in October 2026, former federal appellate judge Alex Kozinski applauded Hegseth’s decision to execute Hasan by firing squad. He was reiterating a view he expressed in a 2014 dissenting opinion: “Eight or ten large-caliber rifle bullets fired at close range can inflict massive damage, causing instant death every time.”

“Sure,” Kozinski added, “firing squads can be messy, but if we are willing to carry out executions, we should not shield ourselves from the reality that we are shedding human blood. If we, as a society, cannot stomach the splatter from an execution carried out by firing squad, then we shouldn’t be carrying out executions at all.”…

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-24 13:12 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The surge of women elected in the 2026 midterms, particularly women of color, will shape political engagement for a generation of young people
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

On the day after the 2026 midterms, Atlanta’s WSB-TV led off its coverage by showing a series of almost entirely white men get replaced, one by one, by Black women.

Not only had Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as the nation’s first Black woman governor, African American women had also won positions as secretary of state, attorney general, state school superintendent, agriculture commissioner, insurance commissioner and labor commissioner.

In the legislative branch, Georgia’s likely incoming speaker of the House of Representatives is also a Black woman. Reporter Candace McEwen, herself a Black woman, ended her report by recounting how her 9-year-old goddaughter, upon seeing the graphic showing all the new Black women leaders in Georgia, commented, “I might have a shot!”

As McEwen concluded: “Indeed she does.”

As political scientists who have long studied the effects of women politicians, our research has shown that both McEwen and her young goddaughter are right: When young people see politicians who look like them, they are inspired to be politically engaged.

‘Inspiration now, participation later’

Following the 2026 midterm elections, a record number of women will serve in state and national offices. More women of color will serve in prominent political offices than ever before.

As of this writing — with some races yet to be called — at least 162 women will serve in the U.S. Congress, 138 of them in the House of Representatives, according to the Center for American Women and Politics.

A minimum of 18 women will serve as governors, while 108 will serve in other statewide executive offices. The new Congress will seat an unprecedented 31 Black, 29 Hispanic, nine Asian American/Pacific Islander and four Native American women, and three women of Middle Eastern heritage.

These women of color will no doubt have significant effects on public policy as they draw on their life experiences while governing. In addition, our research shows that they will have another kind of impact on young people in their states and districts. Specifically, when women run for office, they motivate young girls to get involved in politics.

Women of color, however, are especially inspiring for young girls. Not surprisingly, they serve as role models for young girls of color, igniting their political interest and even leading them to envision themselves as running for office one day.

But their impact also extends to white girls, who are inspired by seeing these women overcome the double barriers of gender and race. This inspiration while young leads to greater political participation in adulthood.

There’s the concrete connection: Inspiration now, participation later.

‘You can’t be what you can’t see’

While teenagers typically do not spend a lot of time following politics, they often absorb lessons from their political environment by osmosis, such as a news story shared on social media, passing by a billboard or holding a conversation with a parent or teacher. Because politics has historically been a man’s game – and a white man’s game at that – seeing women, and women of color especially, in public life changes their default assumption about who is suited to govern.

Politics is no longer just for white men. In the famous words of civil and children’s rights advocate Marian Wright Edelman, you can’t be what you can’t see. When young women see women in positions of leadership, they believe they can be leaders too.

If we left the story here, the election of all these women of color may seem like an unmitigated win for the long-term vitality of American democracy. But the story is a little more complicated.

The historic wave of women is a win for the future of the Democrats specifically. This is because the overwhelming majority of these newly elected women are Democrats.

‘Stunning party imbalance’

Of the 162 women who have officially won their midterm House or Senate races so far, 122 – 75% – of them are Democrats. That’s a stunning party imbalance.

There is an even greater imbalance for women of color. In Georgia, all the African American women elected to statewide office are Democrats. In the U.S. House, all but four of the women of color are Democrats; in the Senate, it’s 100%.

This matters because we have also found that young people are most likely to see candidates from their own party as role models.

Lest you doubt that we can speak of teenagers as Democrats or Republicans, study after study finds that party attachments develop young, and the same polarization found among adults is mirrored in their children.

In other words, the girls who are inspired by this wave of women are far more likely to be Democrats than Republicans. Since partisan teens usually grow up to be partisan adults, this suggests that future Democratic women – whether they be racial minorities or whites – will be more politically engaged in adulthood.

For all the attention paid to the political choices of young Republican men, the party should be worried about the future of Republican women. Without more women politicians representing the GOP, Republican girls are likely to continue seeing politics as a man’s game and stay on the sidelines of civic life.

Evolving perceptions

This doesn’t mean this wave of mostly Democratic women politicians won’t have any impact on Republican teens.

When women of either party run for office, both Republican girls and boys change their attitudes about women.

In general, Republican teens are less likely than Democrats to think that women have the necessary traits to be political leaders. But when they live in a community where women candidates run, they come to see women as fit to govern.

Why the change among Republicans and not Democrats? To be blunt, it is because Democratic kids do not need to be convinced that women are as capable of leadership as men.…

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-24 13:12 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Backlash against data centers helped Democrats win the midterms
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The 2026 midterm elections that swept Democrats into power in Congress and state legislatures also delivered a stunning rebuke to the artificial intelligence industry.

Ballot measures that limited the construction of data centers – from California to Kansas to North Dakota – were approved by voters in 40 of 41 instances. These measures included the Kansas prohibition on construction of a type of battery energy storage system, a 180-day moratorium on data centers in Maine, and the outright ban on data center construction in Ohio.

Drawing on recent survey data, we suggest that the Democratic sweep and the nationwide rejection of data centers are related. Republicans’ connections with an unpopular AI industry may have contributed to their poor showing at the polls.

Bipartisan rejection

We are survey researchers. Our August 2026 survey of a nationally representative sample of 1,000 American adults shows that opposition to data centers is widespread.

The survey shows that 65% of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. This opposition is bipartisan, with 76% of Democrats, 67% of independents and 52% of Republicans opposed to the sites.

To better understand the sources of this opposition, we asked respondents to explain it in their own words. Twenty-eight percent of respondents voiced concerns about the negative environmental impact of data centers. One respondent stated: “Draining our water reserves significantly with a data center would be catastrophic to our region.”

Some respondents, 15%, also expressed concerns about data centers’ negative impact on their quality of life. For example, one respondent said: “Noise issues, energy issues and visual site are three issues that are major concerns for a AI data center to be in the area I live in.”

Ten percent of respondents singled out the centers’ connection to increased utility costs. One respondent said that “ever since a data center has been built in my local area the prices of water and electricity have more than doubled.”

Finally, 13% of respondents expressed a broad distrust of AI and the industry itself, with one stating, “I think that AI needs to be better regulated and a lot more developed and proven safe before any massive full scale deployment.”

A winning issue

Despite mounting public opposition to data centers, President Donald Trump expressed strong support for data center construction before Election Day. He said that if Americans want to live in “crime-infested areas” and “squalor,” they should not have a data center. Days after the midterms, Trump threatened to penalize U.S. companies that build data centers overseas.

As widespread opposition to data centers grew through 2026, Republican congressional candidates increasingly had to weigh loyalty to Trump against local backlash. As Election Day neared, many Republican candidates had distanced themselves from unrestricted data center construction.

In contrast, many Democrats made opposition to data centers an important theme of their campaigns.

Our poll suggests that these efforts may have resonated with voters.

Among Americans who expressed opposition to data centers, 48% indicated they would support the local Democratic candidate in the U.S. House of Representatives, compared to 25% for the Republican candidate. And 47% of those living in states that held a Senate election were planning on voting for the Democratic candidate, while 28% planned to vote for the Republican Senate candidate.

Even taking partisanship, ideology and demographic characteristics into account, opposition to data centers was associated with an intention to support Democratic House and Senate candidates.

Given widespread public concern about data center construction, Democrats have electoral incentives to make AI regulation a part of their legislative agenda in the new Congress. Whether or not they enact new legislation, popular opposition to data centers is unlikely to abate anytime soon.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

J.R.R. Tolkien was a philologist by trade, and he wove his deep knowledge of language into every book in his Lord of the Rings universe.Â

Many of the names he used in The Hobbit stem from Old Norse and Old English, but by the time The Lord of the Rings was published, he had largely completed the basic structure of his original Elvish languages, Quenya and Sindarin, along with elements of numerous others.

These invented languages were central to his work. âThe invention of languages is the foundation,â he wrote. âThe âstoriesâ were made rather to provide a world for the languages than the reverse. To me a name comes first and the story follows.â

These original languages also provided the basis for many of his major charactersâ names. Aragornâs name translates to ârevered kingâ in Sindarin, and Galadriel means âmaiden crowned with a radiant garlandâ in the same language. Sauronâs name translates to âThe Abhorredâ in Quenya, and Legolas means âgreen foliageâ in Sindarin. Arwen translates to ânoble maidenâ in the same language, though this name has also been linked to Welsh names such as Arwyn, which is said to mean âfairâ or âblessed.â

Still other charactersâ names are rooted in ancient languages and mythology. One thing that unites all of Tolkienâs names, however, is that he chose them with great care. Tolkien was so meticulous and intentional about his naming process that he wrote an entire handbook called Guide to the Names in âThe Lord of the Rings,â which detailed exactly which names ought to be translated and how.

Even so, the precise roots of many of Tolkienâs most famous charactersâ names remain unclear. This has led scholars and readers to speculate tirelessly about how the author came up with the names of his legendary cast of villains, kings, and reluctant heroes.Â

Bilbo Baggins

In general, Tolkien imbued all his charactersâ names with deep meaningâbut one apparent exception is Bilbo, the hero of The Hobbit. âTo their man-children they usually gave names that had no meaning at all in their daily language; and some of their women's names were similar,â Tolkien wrote in Appendix F in The Lord of the Rings. âOf this kind are Bilbo, Bungo, Polo, Lotho, Tanta, Nina, and so on.â (Perhaps, of course, the randomness of Bilboâs name fits a hero whose identity is closely tied to his everyman nature, at least at first.)Â

Baggins had more intention behind it. âIntended to recall âbag,ââ Tolkien wrote in Guide to the Names in âLord of the Rings,â adding that any translation of this surname should include an element meaning âsackâ or âbag.â He also added that the surname is â...meant to be associated (by hobbits) with Bag End (that is, the end of a 'bag' or 'pudding bag' = culde-sac [sic]), the local name for Bilbo's house.â Bag End, the author added, was the name of his auntâs farm in Dormston, Worcestershire. Tolkien visited often as a child, and the small, cozy rooms he found there helped give shape to the Shire (and clearly, the Baggins family name).

Ãowyn

Tolkien is widely believed to have invented the name of the heroic noblewoman Ãowyn by combining the Old English word eoh, meaning horse, with wynn, meaning joy. Additionally, it has been noted that the name Ãwyn has Celtic origins and is related to the name Eoghan, which means âborn of yewâ in Irish Gaelic, though no clear connection between these names and Eowyn's has been established.

Gandalf

Gandalf is an ancient and powerful wizard whose influence reaches across the world of The Lord of the Rings. The name âGandalfâ stems from the Old Norse name GandÃ¡lfr, which translates to âwand-elfâ; gandr means wand, staff, or magic, and Ã¡lfr means elf. Tolkien took the name from the VÃ¶luspÃ¡, the best-known work of the Poetic Edda, a series of anonymous Old Norse narrative poems that serves as the basis of Norse-Icelandic mythology.

In The Lord of the Rings, Gandalf is a name given to the wizard by the Men of the North. Gandalf is known by several names across Middle-earth. His Elvish name is Mithrandir, which translates to âGrey Pilgrimâ in Sindarin. His real name is OlÃ³rin, which means âdreamâ or âvisionâ in Quenya, an ancient, formal Elvish language.

Gollum

In The Hobbit, Tolkien shares that Gollumâs name came from the character's tendency to make âa horrible swallowing noise in his throat.â Scholars have a variety of theories as to how the author actually came up with this evocative moniker. One suggests Tolkien may have been inspired by the Old Norse word gull or goll, which means âgold.â Another proposes that he may have been influenced by the Hebrew word golem, which refers to an unformed body in the Bible and describes an animated figure made from clay or lifeless matter in Jewish folklore.Â

Before he was twisted into Gollum by the pull of the One Ring, Gollum was a Hobbit named SmÃ©agol. Some linguists have theorized that this name comes from the Old English word smÃ©ah, which means âcreeping inâ or âpenetrating,â or the related Old English smÃ©agan, which means âto ponderâ or âto scrutinize.â

Frodo

Tolkien took the name of the Lord of the Ringsâ central hero from FrÃ³Ã°i, the name of several kings often said to be descended from the god Odin in Norse mythology. This name translates to âwiseâ or âclever,â and has been spelled âFrotho,â âFrode,â or âFrodoâ in various contexts. Many Norse stories focus on the Danish King FrÃ³Ã°i, who is said to have been such a noble and wise leader that, according to one account, if a golden ring was left outside during his reign, no one would steal it. Interestingly, Frodoâs name wasnât always set in stone; in early drafts, Tolkien called him Bingo Bolger Baggins.Â

Saruman

The villainous Saruman the Whiteâs name likely comes from the Old English word searu, which translates to âcunningâ or âskilled.â Tolkien used Old English for the dialect of the Northmen of Middle-earth, and Saruman is this groupâs translation of the wizardâs original Elvish name, Curumo, which means âskilled manâ in Quenya.…

item.title: These are the 17 greatest spy movies of all time – how many have you watched?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

These are the 17 greatest spy movies of all time – how many have you watched?

From suspenseful Hitchcock masterpieces to thrilling James Bond blockbusters, the espionage genre has gripped viewers for more than a century. Paul Burke names the films you can’t afford to miss

With actor Robert Pattinson recently announced as the next James Bond, after much media and fan speculation, Ian Fleming’s iconic secret agent is set to return to the silver screen. The global appetite for spy stories is clearly insatiable. But what keeps us coming back?

Espionage cinema is more than gadgets and gunfights, false identities and coded messages: it mirrors the fears and obsessions of its time. Hitchcock’s thrillers tapped into the threat of invasion; John le Carré’s Cold War dramas exposed the moral compromises of espionage; and today’s films grapple with terrorism, surveillance and cyberwarfare.

But where should you turn for high-octane thrills, gripping conflict or savage satires? From Bond and Bourne to Smiley and a few less familiar agents, which films deserve to be called the greatest spy films ever made? These are 17 of the finest examples...

1. The 39 Steps

(Alfred Hitchcock, 1935)

The master of suspense, Alfred Hitchcock, clinches the award for the first great espionage movie.

Richard Hannay (Robert Donat) is bored by London, but a chance meeting with agent-in-hiding Annabella Smith (Lucie Mannheim) changes everything. When she is murdered in his flat, Hannay finds himself the chief suspect and soon on the run from the police.

Forced to prove his innocence, he falls foul of a spy ring selling secret plans to a mysterious foreign power. Fleeing to Scotland with reluctant accomplice Pamela (Madeleine Carroll), Hannay seeks out his unknown enemy to clear his name.

Hitchcock blends suspense, romance and sly comedy to create a timeless thriller, edging out his other prewar classic The Lady Vanishes. Look out for the music hall finale.

2. Casablanca

(Michael Curtiz, 1942)

Everybody comes to Rick’s Café Américain: it’s the most fashionable watering hole in Vichy-controlled Casablanca. Rick (Humphrey Bogart) has been drowning his sorrows ever since Ilsa (Ingrid Bergman) jilted him in Paris as the Germans invaded. Returning two years later with her husband, Victor Laszlo (Paul Henreid), the most wanted resistance fighter in Nazi Europe, Ilsa turns to Rick to help Victor escape to America. But can he put heartbreak aside?

Michael Curtiz’s film follows the sacrifice and courage of the love triangle against the backdrop of war. The “hill of beans” speech will melt you if the singing of the ‘Marseillaise’ hasn’t done that already. Transcending wartime propaganda, Curtiz’s film is a cinematic masterpiece.

3. Notorious

(Alfred Hitchcock, 1946)

Following the Second World War, Hitchcock, now in Hollywood, continued to explore the story of ordinary people caught up in momentous events.

Alicia Huberman (Ingrid Bergman), daughter of a convicted Nazi, is recruited by US agent TR Devlin (Cary Grant) to infiltrate Nazi fugitives hiding in Rio. Her mission is to rekindle her relationship with the group’s leader, Alexander Sebastian (Claude Rains). The complication? Devlin has fallen for Alicia himself.

Gripping and passionate, Notorious explores the personal cost of duty and the compromises it demands.

4. The Third Man

(Carol Reed, 1949)

This regularly tops the lists of greatest movies of all time and for good reason: Carol Reed’s adaptation of Graham Greene’s story is a convincing portrait of Vienna and early Cold War Europe.

American writer Holly Martins (Joseph Cotten) arrives for a job in the postwar city under the control of the Allied powers. He finds that his would-be employer and long-time friend Harry Lime (Orson Welles) was killed in a car accident the day before.

The British authorities, to Martins’s disbelief, accuse Lime of selling diluted penicillin, putting children’s lives at risk. Martins investigates, even as he falls for Lime’s girlfriend Anna (Alida Valli), and his loyalty is tested as he seeks justice for the victims of the black-market racket.

From the haunting zither soundtrack to the exhilarating scene in the sewers, this is a classy film.

5. North by Northwest

(Alfred Hitchcock, 1959)

The final Hitchcock gem of this list sees advertising executive Roger Thornhill (Cary Grant) facing a case of mistaken identity which makes him the target of a spy ring. Pursued across America, Thornhill encounters secret agents, shifting loyalties and the mysterious Eve Kendall (Eva Marie Saint), whose motives are unclear.

Grant’s comic timing as an ordinary man trying to survive a plot he barely understands stands the test of time and the Mount Rushmore climax is one of cinema’s most iconic scenes. A dazzling adventure that helped define the big-screen spy thriller.

6. From Russia with Love

(Terence Young, 1963)

This Terence Young movie is my favourite Bond, just edging out Goldfinger and Dr No. Your favourite 007 is probably the actor you first saw in the part and for me it was Sean Connery.

Bond travels to Istanbul to steal a Soviet Lektor decoder machine with the help of Russian clerk Tatiana (Daniela Bianchi). But she has been hoodwinked by SPECTRE agent Rosa Klebb (Lotte Lenya), who plans to kill Bond and seize the device. Klebb and deadly assassin Grant (Robert Shaw) follow them from Istanbul to Venice in a film that delivers glamour, action, humour and romance.

Pacy, slightly tongue-in-cheek, it continues to delight audiences today.

7. The Ipcress File

(Sidney J Furie, 1965)

James Bond may have defined glamorous espionage, but Sidney J Furie’s witty thriller was a genuine game changer. Michael Caine plays Harry Palmer, a cheeky working-class squaddie caught stealing and subsequently blackmailed into being a spy. He is tasked with finding a missing nuclear scientist and in the process uncovers a secret brainwashing programme: IPCRESS.…
